title: A threshold does not specify a yield
question: What can energy conservation say about gas ionization?
recap: Under a one-quantum ionization assumption, a quantum must meet the required ionization energy. Absorbed energy bounds the count; equality requires that every absorbed quantum causes exactly one counted ionization.
premises: One quantum supplies the ionization energy in the stated idealization.
Only the absorbed energy counts, not all the energy that arrives.
A count equality requires one counted ionization per absorbed quantum.
limitations: A threshold is a necessary energy condition, not a material cross-section or a guaranteed event.
An unknown absorbed fraction or yield is never silently taken to be 100 percent.
The energy budget does not predict recombination, collisions, or avalanche multiplication.

overview.text: Under a one-quantum ionization assumption, a quantum must meet the required ionization energy. Absorbed energy bounds the count; equality requires that every absorbed quantum causes exactly one counted ionization.

full.text: Let \(I\) be the required energy for the specified ionization channel. A single quantum can pay this cost only when \(h\nu\) is at least \(I\). A smaller quantum leaves an energy deficit; a larger quantum makes the event energetically possible, not certain.

full.spoken: One-quantum ionization requires quantum energy at least equal to the specified ionization energy.

full.text: For monochromatic absorbed energy \(E_\text{abs}\), the number of absorbed quanta is represented by \(E_\text{abs}/(h\nu)\). With at most one counted ionization per quantum this gives an upper bound. It becomes an equality only when all absorbed quanta each produce one counted ionization.

full.spoken: The ionization count is at most absorbed energy divided by quantum energy, under the at-most-one-ionization assumption.

full.text: The ionization laboratory separates incident energy, absorbed fraction, threshold, and conversion assumptions. Its historical checks use their own stated units; this explanation does not infer a new gas species or a real-material yield from a threshold slider.

full.returnCaption: Return to the energy threshold and the separately conditioned count bound.

steps.text: Letters: the paper writes J for the work needed to ionize one gram-equivalent, L for the amount of light absorbed (not the speed of light here), and j for the number of gram-molecules ionized. This explanation works per molecule: I is the energy needed to ionize one molecule, hν is one quantum, \(E_{\mathrm{abs}}\) is the absorbed energy, and \(n_{\mathrm{ions}}\) is the count of ions.

items: The assumption: when a gas is ionized by ultraviolet light, each absorbed quantum is used to ionize one gas molecule.
A single quantum can pay the cost of ionization only if it carries at least that much energy. Per molecule, that is the formula below.

steps.spoken: One-quantum ionization requires quantum energy at least equal to the specified ionization energy.

items: The paper's form, for one gram-equivalent: multiply both sides by N, and the condition reads Rβν at least J.

Worked with the paper's inputs. Lenard's longest wavelength that still ionizes air is about \(1{,}9\cdot10^{-5}\) cm. Its frequency is the speed of light divided by the wavelength, \(3\times10^{10}/(1.9\times10^{-5})=1.58\times10^{15}\) per second. Then Rβν is \(8.31\times10^{7}\times4.866\times10^{-11}\times1.58\times10^{15}=6.4\times10^{12}\) erg, with R the standard value of 1905; the page prints \(6{,}4\cdot10^{12}\) erg.

So J is at most about \(6.4\times10^{12}\) erg per gram-equivalent. An independent upper bound comes from Stark's smallest measured ionizing voltage for air, about 10 volts: 10 volts times the charge of a gram-equivalent, \(9.6\times10^{3}\) electromagnetic units, is \(10\times10^{8}\times9.6\times10^{3}=9.6\times10^{12}\) erg. The paper remarks that the two bounds are nearly equal.
Now the count. With light of one frequency, the absorbed energy divided by the energy of one quantum is the number of quanta absorbed.
If each absorbed quantum ionizes at most one molecule, the number of ions cannot exceed that number of quanta.

steps.spoken: The ionization count is at most absorbed energy divided by quantum energy, under the at-most-one-ionization assumption.

items: The paper's stronger statement assumes exactly one ionization for each absorbed quantum: \(j=L/(R\beta\nu)\) gram-molecules for absorbed light L. It states the condition: the gas must show, at that frequency, no noticeable absorption that is not accompanied by ionization.

Worked count: absorb 1 erg of light at Lenard's limit. Per molecule, one quantum carries \(6.4\times10^{12}/(6.17\times10^{23})=1.03\times10^{-11}\) erg, so 1 erg is about \(9.7\times10^{10}\) quanta, and at most that many ions.
Meeting the threshold makes an ionization possible, not certain. An unknown absorbed fraction or yield stays unknown rather than being set to 100 percent.
The paper calls a test of this count by experiment very important, and ends there, dated Bern, 17 March 1905.

margin.text: §9 applies the same bound to gases ionized by ultraviolet light: at most one molecule ionized for each absorbed quantum, and none unless the quantum carries at least the ionization energy. The paper ends after this section, with its date-line.
